title: TaskCompletionSource and manual task completion (bridging callbacks to await)
hook: Not every async API returns a Task. TaskCompletionSource lets you create a Task you complete yourself — the bridge between callback-based SDKs and await.

blocks.text: TaskCompletionSource<T> (or the non-generic TaskCompletionSource) is a factory for a Task whose completion you control manually. Call SetResult, SetException, or SetCanceled when your callback fires, a timer expires, or a message arrives on a socket. The returned Task is awaitable like any other. This is how you wrap legacy event-based APIs, coordinate multiple async signals, or implement timeout-with-fallback patterns without blocking.

entries.plainDefinition: A class that creates a Task and lets you complete it later with result, exception, or cancellation.
Transitions the Task to RanToCompletion with the given result. Can only be called once.
Like SetResult but returns false if the Task was already completed — safe for racing callbacks.
Using TCS to signal one waiter when an external event occurs — cleaner than polling.
entries.example: await tcs.Task; // resumes when callback calls SetResult

blocks.text: AWS SDK v2 callbacks, raw WebSocket events, and third-party libraries that only expose Action<T> completion handlers cannot be awaited directly. TaskCompletionSource is the standard .NET bridge. In production you also use it for single-flight deduplication (ConcurrentDictionary<string, TaskCompletionSource<T>>), racing a Redis timeout against a slow HTTP call, or signaling that a background worker finished initialization before the host accepts traffic.

blocks.title: Prefer TrySet over Set
blocks.body: Racing callbacks (timeout vs success) will call completion twice. TrySetResult and TrySetException return false on the loser instead of throwing InvalidOperationException.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Bridging a callback API to await

items.title: Register the callback
items.body: Pass a lambda to the legacy API that calls tcs.TrySetResult or TrySetException.

items.title: Return or await tcs.Task
items.body: Callers await the Task property — it completes when the callback fires.

items.title: Handle timeout or cancellation
items.body: Link a CancellationTokenRegistration or CancelAfter to call TrySetCanceled.

snippet.label: Wrap a callback-based HTTP client
snippet.explanation: RunContinuationsAsynchronously prevents the callback thread from running continuations inline — important when the callback fires on a UI or I/O thread you do not want to block.

snippet.label: Race HTTP against a timeout with TCS
snippet.explanation: The TCS Task completes with result, exception, or cancellation. TrySet methods handle the race between timeout and success safely.

snippet.label: Single-flight cache load per key
snippet.explanation: Multiple concurrent callers for the same key share one TCS-backed Task. Only the first load runs; others await the same completion.

snippet.label: Failure mode: SetResult twice throws
snippet.explanation: SetResult and SetException throw if the Task is already completed. Production code with racing signals must use TrySet variants.

blocks.title: Manual promise completion vs TaskCompletionSource
rows: No built-in cancel — use AbortSignal separately
resolve after resolve is silently ignored
Microtasks always async on same thread

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling SetResult twice when timeout and success race — use TrySet. Forgetting RunContinuationsAsynchronously and blocking the callback thread with heavy continuations. Leaking TCS instances in a dictionary without TryRemove on completion. Creating a new TCS per call when Task.FromResult would suffice for already-complete values.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: TaskCompletionSource is the implementation detail behind many framework APIs — ManualResetEventSlim's async variants, Channel readers, and HttpClient's internal completion sources. Under load, a leaked TCS in an in-flight dictionary shows up as growing gen-2 heap and Tasks that never complete. Use dotnet-counters to watch thread-pool queue length when continuations run synchronously on callback threads (missing RunContinuationsAsynchronously). BenchmarkDotNet comparing Task.FromResult vs new TCS for sync-complete paths shows when TCS is unnecessary overhead.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'I use TaskCompletionSource everywhere' without distinguishing it from Task.FromResult. Calling SetResult in a timeout handler without TrySet and crashing on the success path that already completed. Not mentioning RunContinuationsAsynchronously when wrapping UI-thread callbacks. Confusing TCS with Task.Run — TCS does not queue work to the pool; it only signals completion.

interviewTakeaways: TaskCompletionSource creates a Task you complete manually — the bridge from callbacks to await.
Use TrySetResult/TrySetException when timeout and success race; Set throws on double completion.
In production, pair TCS with ConcurrentDictionary for single-flight per-key deduplication under Redis cache stampede.

60s: TaskCompletionSource wraps callback APIs into awaitable Tasks. Use TrySet for racing completions. RunContinuationsAsynchronously keeps callback threads free. Task.FromResult is enough when the value is already known.
Follow-up: how does IValueTaskSource relate to TCS for zero-allocation hot paths?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'TCS is just Task.Run' gets you rejected — TCS signals completion; it does not schedule work.
Calling SetResult twice in a timeout race instead of TrySetResult — production crash on the losing path.
Strong answer: 'I use TCS to bridge legacy callbacks and for single-flight deduplication; sync-complete paths use Task.FromResult or ValueTask instead.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: The Promise constructor executor is the JS equivalent of TaskCompletionSource: you hold resolve/reject and call them when an external event fires. C# adds explicit cancellation via TrySetCanceled and RunContinuationsAsynchronously for thread control.
Many TS codebases wrap { promise, resolve, reject } in a Deferred helper — identical pattern to TCS. C# TCS is built into the BCL with TrySet safety and TaskCreationOptions.
